analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on Nipah virus (Henipavirus nipahense), Nipah virus infection and disease. The central question is the development of broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals (BSAs) against RNA viruses, including Nipah virus, with activity spanning multiple genera, entire families, or even crossing viral families.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a systematic overview of approved and investigational antiviral agents active against RNA viruses, including Nipah virus. It discusses the rationale for developing BSAs and outlines the biological determinants underlying their antiviral spectrum. The review does not explicitly report on meta-analysis or pooled estimates but provides a non-exhaustive overview of existing and experimental drugs.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that the development of broader-acting small molecule antivirals is essential to address current unmet medical needs and to strengthen epidemic and pandemic preparedness. It highlights that newly emerging viruses are likely to belong to known viral families, supporting the strategy of developing BSAs. The review also outlines the clinical development frameworks required to evaluate such drugs, particularly in outbreaks.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review identifies a lack of effective antiviral therapeutics for many RNA viruses, including Nipah virus, as a major evidence gap. It notes that while advances in metagenomics and high-throughput sequencing have expanded our understanding of viral diversity, the development of BSAs remains limited. The review also highlights the need for more research on the biological determinants that underlie the antiviral spectrum of these drugs.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review emphasizes the need for sustained investment in antiviral drug discovery, particularly for RNA viruses like Nipah virus. It suggests that developing potent, safe, and orally available antivirals is crucial for both treating known viral infections and responding rapidly to outbreaks. The review also outlines the importance of clinical development frameworks tailored for BSAs.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the development of broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals (BSAs) against RNA viruses, with a focus on Nipah virus. It highlights the lack of effective antiviral treatments for many RNA viruses, including Nipah, and underscores the importance of creating drugs with activity spanning multiple genera or families. The review discusses the rationale for BSAs, the biological factors influencing their antiviral spectrum, and the clinical frameworks needed to evaluate them. papers.title: Epitope and immunological basis for superior immunogenicity of henipavirus glycoprotein HeV.G over NiV.G in mRNA vaccines
papers.abstract: Nipah (NiV) and Hendra (HeV) viruses are highly lethal zoonotic Henipaviruses with pandemic potential, for which no licensed vaccines exist. The surface glycoprotein (G) is the primary target of neutralizing antibodies, yet a systematic comparison of the immunogenicity of NiV.G and HeV.G has been lacking. Here, we engineered mRNA vaccines encoding the full-length G proteins of NiV and HeV. In Syrian hamsters, while both vaccines conferred homologous protection, only HeV.G vaccination at a lower dose (5 μg) provided complete cross-protection against lethal NiV challenge. Comparative immune profiling revealed that HeV.G vaccination induced significantly higher neutralizing antibody titers, which correlated with robust germinal center B cell expansion and a stronger CD4 + T follicular helper (Tfh) cell response, despite equivalent B cell activation. Epitope mapping uncovered a structurally conserved yet immunologically divergent MHC class II-restricted peptide (YIAITKVER) in HeV.G with superior predicted binding affinity, providing a mechanistic basis for the enhanced T cell help. Our work establishes HeV.G as a superior vaccine immunogen due to its distinct epitope repertoire and underscores the critical role of CD4 + T cell help in driving cross-protective B cell immunity. We further developed a bivalent vaccine Gmix, which induced balanced antibody and cellular immune responses against both G proteins, thereby confirming the value of multivalent vaccines in broadening immune coverage. Collectively, this study defines HeV.G as the preferred antigen for pan-henipavirus vaccine development and offers a framework for rational antigen selection against future viral threats.

It highlights the lack of systematic comparison between NiV.G and HeV.G, despite their shared status as highly lethal zoonotic Henipaviruses. It also suggests the potential of multivalent vaccines in broadening immune coverage. The findings do not report specific limitations, but the evidence is strong due to the direct comparison of immunogenicity and mechanistic insights.

papers.source_body_en: Nipah (NiV) and Hendra (HeV) viruses are highly lethal zoonotic Henipaviruses with pandemic potential, for which no licensed vaccines exist. The surface glycoprotein (G) is the primary target of neutralizing antibodies, yet a systematic comparison of the immunogenicity of NiV.G and HeV.G has been lacking. Here, we engineered mRNA vaccines encoding the full-length G proteins of NiV and HeV. In Syrian hamsters, while both vaccines conferred homologous protection, only HeV.G vaccination at a lower dose (5 μg) provided complete cross-protection against lethal NiV challenge. Comparative immune profiling revealed that HeV.G vaccination induced significantly higher neutralizing antibody titers, which correlated with robust germinal center B cell expansion and a stronger CD4 + T follicular helper (Tfh) cell response, despite equivalent B cell activation. Epitope mapping uncovered a structurally conserved yet immunologically divergent MHC class II-restricted peptide (YIAITKVER) in HeV.G with superior predicted binding affinity, providing a mechanistic basis for the enhanced T cell help. Our work establishes HeV.G as a superior vaccine immunogen due to its distinct epitope repertoire and underscores the critical role of CD4 + T cell help in driving cross-protective B cell immunity. We further developed a bivalent vaccine Gmix, which induced balanced antibody and cellular immune responses against both G proteins, thereby confirming the value of multivalent vaccines in broadening immune coverage. Collectively, this study defines HeV.G as the preferred antigen for pan-henipavirus vaccine development and offers a framework for rational antigen selection against future viral threats.

papers.full_text: ABSTRACTIntroductionZoonotic diseases pose risks to human, animal, and ecosystem health; effective management relies on coordinated actions across sectors. Although One Health principles promote collaboration across sectors, operational tools for multisectoral risk assessment (RA) are lacking. Therefore, the Tripartite (FAO, WHO, and WOAH) developed the first‐ever One Health operational tool for Joint Risk Assessment (JRA‐OT), with inputs from 15 pilot countries and international experts. This article describes how information from pilots in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia contributed to informing co‐development of the final JRA process and tool.MethodsThree in‐person meetings with international RA and zoonotic disease experts with a One Health background were convened in Rome, Italy, to co‐develop the methodology (November 2017, September 2018) and incorporate pilot feedback (February 2020). Development criteria included a standard, systematic, qualitative, and multisectoral RA process, facilitating incorporation of expert opinion and sector‐specific RA results. The pilot workshops described here were conducted in Indonesia (March 2018), the United Republic of Tanzania (March 2019), and Georgia (July 2019), and feedback was incorporated iteratively into the JRA‐OT by a Tripartite Secretariat.ResultsThese pilot workshops demonstrated JRA's utility and provided critical information for improvements. Key findings included the (1) value of policy‐level risk framing, (2) importance of political will, (3) need for subnational engagement, (4) importance of including all relevant sectors, and (5) necessity of clear, stepwise guidance to facilitate efficient collaboration and support training of national trainers.ConclusionsCo‐development of the JRA using country pilots and expert consultations allowed for field‐testing and iterative improvement of the tool, ensuring incorporation of user requirements, robust methodology for the joint, multisectoral assessment of national zoonotic disease risks, and ownership by the different sectors. The process serves as a model for co‐development of other multisectoral operational tools.Keywords: Joint Operational Tools, One Health, risk assessment, zoonoses Piloting of the Tripartite Joint Risk Assessment (JRA) process and tool in countries provided feedback for improvement, evidence‐based estimates of national risks from priority zoonotic diseases, and practical training of national facilitators. The JRA offers simple step‐by‐step guidance to countries wishing to undertake joint qualitative risk assessments. 2.Methods2.1.Initial Tool DevelopmentThe JRA‐OT development began in 2014 and was led by a multisectoral international team of epidemiologists, zoonotic disease experts, and RA experts from six countries in three regions, including many from this team of authors, convened through virtual meetings. They reviewed and examined existing sector‐specific RA methods and tools for their suitability and relevance and agreed on the following criteria for the joint RA: Provide a standard, systematic process for conducting evidence‐based RA on joint priority zoonotic disease hazards.Be qualitative and facilitate incorporation of expert opinion when only minimal and/or poor‐quality data are available.Allow identification of data gaps, and benefit from iterative use as additional data becomes available.Promote use of data and results from sector‐specific RAs.Provide step‐by‐step operational guidance to facilitate effective and equitable collaboration and sharing of information, expertise, and perspectives.Be prospectively joint across all relevant sectors, that is, public health (e.g., ministries of health, public health agencies), animal health (e.g., veterinary services), environmental (e.g., wildlife health, environmental protection agencies), and others, such as security and disaster services.Function within existing zoonotic disease management and One Health governance infrastructures.Be adaptable to the relevant contextBe usable by governments, academia, or anyone wishing to conduct RA jointly across sectors.Support international sector‐specific RA and health security frameworks (e.g., International Health Regulations [9], WHO Rapid RA [4], WOAH Import Risk Analysis [5], FAO draft Guidelines on Rapid RA [now published [6]]).Once the new basic JRA process and tool were agreed, they were tested during (1) two international in‐person workshops in Rome, Italy (November 2017, September 2018), bringing together international multisectoral RA experts from different geographical regions selected by the three organizations to review and fine‐tune the methodology, and (2) 15 country pilots conducted between March 2018 and December 2019 (Figure 1), which guided iterative updates. All pilots were in‐person and had the same direct and indirect objectives (Table 1). A final in‐person expert consultation was held in Rome, Italy (February 2020), and the JRA‐OT was published in December 2020 [8]. The development timeline is depicted in Figure 2.FIGURE 1Joint Risk Assessment pilot countries.TABLE 1Objectives of the Joint Risk Assessment (JRA) pilot workshops.Direct objectivesIndirect objectives Build capacity through training a pool of national facilitators to operationalize the JRA tool at national and subnational levelsProvide likelihood and impact estimates for risk assessment questions on priority hazardsAssess the usefulness of the JRA and consider its sustained useCollect feedback to improve interim versions of the JRA Enhance coordination and trust among relevant stakeholdersFacilitate official and unofficial communication and information sharing among stakeholdersAdvocate for allocation of resources FIGURE 2Development timeline of the Joint Risk Assessment operational tool.2.2.Pilot WorkshopsFor each of the 15 pilot workshops, all relevant ministries, particularly those responsible for animal health and public health, were encouraged to engage through outreach by FAO and WHO country offices. Tripartite central, regional, and country office staff supported the workshops as external facilitators. All pilots, aside from the Indonesian pilot where the risk framing was conducted during the workshop, followed the six steps, below and in Figure 3, adapted from common RA processes used in public health, animal health, and/or environmental RA: Hazard identification: Technical staff and decision‐makers in engaged ministries (hereafter, “ministries”) agreed on national priority endemic, epidemic, or emerging zoonotic hazards, up to 6 months prior to the workshop. Risk framing: Once the hazards were agreed, ministerial decision‐makers characterized the scope, purpose, and objectives of the assessment on the basis of government strategy and policy to ensure the JRA process remained efficient and focused on critical government needs. Selection of participants and national staff: After Steps 1 and 2, ministries identified participants based on the identified hazards and risk framing and selected staff to facilitate the planning and implementation of the pilot and future JRAs (hereafter, “national facilitators”). A JRA lead was agreed among ministries. High‐level ministerial participation was encouraged for workshop Days 0 and 3. Day 0: National facilitators finalized the risk framing and were trained on the JRA process and tool by the external facilitators. Days 1–2: The JRA was introduced and undertaken by participants, led by the national facilitators and supported by external facilitators. Small groups each focused on one identified hazard using information brought to the workshop and presented the outcome of each step in plenary. Substantial time was dedicated to plenary discussion and questions, covering both the technical assessments and the JRA process itself. Day 3: Each group presented final results in plenary. Participants, including decision‐makers, considered existing national zoonotic disease and One Health infrastructure and options for governance of routine JRA leadership and implementation, and identified what criteria would trigger conducting or updating a JRA.FIGURE 3Schematic of the final Joint Risk Assessment process applied during national JRA pilots. Steps are fully described in WHO et al. [8].2.3.Data Capture, Analysis, and IntegrationFrom each pilot's planning period through to the end of each workshop, constraints, challenges, and proposed solutions gleaned from plenary and group workshop discussions, and verbal feedback from participants and national facilitators were captured in written notes taken by the external facilitators. Standardized written feedback on the process, tool, and workshop was requested anonymously from attendees using a questionnaire (Pilot Feedback Form; see Supporting Information). Completion of questionnaires was optional.At the end of each workshop day, the external and national facilitators gathered to discuss how the day went and share the feedback received so far. Potential modifications to the JRA based on captured information and challenges were continually discussed among the pilot facilitators and the Tripartite focal points leading the development of the JRA (hereafter, JRA Secretariat). After each pilot workshop, the JRA Secretariat met virtually to revisit the feedback received and suggest corrective actions to the tool and process accordingly. On the basis of importance, urgency, and complexity, straightforward and uncontroversial corrections were made by the JRA Secretariat immediately and prior to the next workshop, whereas more complex issues were collected in a list of discussion points and brought forward to expert review and decision during the final expert workshop held in Rome (September 2018). As pilots were conducted, the JRA Secretariat noted that challenges fell into three categories: Challenges that were consistent across countries, such as misleading or unclear text, and definitely required changing to ensure comprehension.Challenges that varied across countries and could not be improved in a generic way and were best managed by stating in JRA materials that these aspects are country‐specific and would be managed during national JRAs.Challenges that fell outside the scope of the JRA process and would not be useful to address in the tool.2.4.Country Pilot Selection for This ManuscriptThe pilots in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia (Table 2 and further described chronologically below) were purposively selected by the JRA Secretariat for further description in this manuscript, based on (1) each being the first country in its geographical region to conduct a JRA pilot and (2) the level of contribution the country's findings had in informing the final JRA content and processes.TABLE 2Summary of Joint Risk Assessment pilot workshops in Indonesia, Tanzania, and Georgia.IndonesiaTanzaniaGeorgiaDatesMarch 13–16, 2018March 25–28, 2019July 2–5, 2019LocationBogorDar es SalaamKakhetiNumber of participants642425Hazards assessedZoonotic influenza viruses, rabies virus, Leptospira interrogans Zoonotic influenza viruses, rabies virus, Bacillus anthracis Rabies virus, Crimean Congo hemorrhagic fever virus Supplementary Materials Supporting File: puh270398‐sup‐0001‐SuppMat.pdf. 3.Results3.1.IndonesiaThe Indonesian JRA pilot workshop was the first JRA pilot conducted and took place in Bogor on March 13–16, 2018. The 64 participants included representatives from central government ministries spanning human and animal health, forestry and environment, security and disasters, the Coordinating Ministry of Human Development and Culture, and health and livestock disease investigation staff from three provinces. Five hazards (zoonotic influenza viruses in three different contexts, rabies virus, and Leptospira interrogans) were assessed. Leveraging the strong multisectoral engagement and zoonotic disease experience of local partners facilitated the emergence of important lessons. Because Indonesia was the first pilot, these lessons greatly impacted the JRA process and tool and all subsequent pilots.The Indonesia pilot generated key findings related to risk framing, pre‐workshop training, political will, and subnational involvement.3.1.1.Introducing a Risk‐Framing StepInitially, the draft JRA process did not include a step where decision‐makers could provide strategic and policy‐related inputs to frame the assessment. As such, Indonesian participants and facilitators found they had to identify the assessment's scope and policy objectives as a first step of the group work. This was time‐consuming and only possible because ministerial decision‐makers were present and engaged to advise. The national facilitators suggested that ministerial decision‐makers could undertake this step prior to the workshop, inspiring the addition of the pre‐pilot risk‐framing step to the final JRA.3.1.2.Adding a 1‐Day Pre‐Workshop Training for National FacilitatorsInitially, the “Day 0 national facilitators” training was also not part of the JRA process. Proactively, the Indonesian organizers initiated a full‐day pre‐pilot meeting of the JRA Secretariat and national technical staff to familiarize national facilitators with the JRA steps and to review the workshop objectives. These included staff from the provinces, and hereafter, the term “national facilitators” is inclusive of subnational staff. The entire team agreed that this pre‐pilot meeting was critical to the success of the workshop as it ensured that national facilitators (1) understood the JRA principles, step‐wise process, and tool; (2) practiced facilitation skills with support from the external facilitators prior to the workshop; and (3) could take a leading role in facilitation the next day. Skilled national facilitators would not only bring local context and perspectives but also create JRA sustainability, as external facilitators would no longer be needed for subsequent national and subnational JRAs. Subsequently, “Day 0” was incorporated for all future pilots, with national facilitators and JRA Secretariat attending Days 0–3 and all other participants attending Days 1–3. “Day 0” is not included in the tool as the JRA is meant to be done autonomously by countries, that is, once facilitators are familiar with the JRA tool and process.3.1.3.Importance of Political Will for JRA SuccessThe Government of Indonesia (GOI) was the first government to request a JRA workshop in 2017. The Ministry of Health (MoH), Ministry of Agriculture (MoA), and Coordinating Ministry of Human Development and Culture (Kemenko PMK) were strongly involved in planning and implementation. Director‐level representatives from these agencies were present during the entire workshop, contributed operationally to discussions, and were available to support the unanticipated risk‐framing activity. Not only did the Director General of MoH Prevention and Disease Control open the JRA, but he also requested a side meeting with the JRA Secretariat to show his direct support and appreciation of the JRA initiative and One Health approaches in general. The team agreed that this high‐level political engagement, as well as leveraging the strong national One Health culture, facilitated the later implementation of JRAs at national and subnational levels [10, 11]. The MoH proposed translating and adapting the tool further for the Indonesian context and embedding JRA within the national and provincial frameworks for zoonoses and other emerging infectious diseases based on the existing infrastructure and legal framework. This would be coordinated centrally by Kemenko PMK in collaboration with MoH, MoA, and Ministry of Environment and Forestry. Political will is now highlighted in the final JRA tool as a key element for enhancing the JRA success.3.1.4.Subnational Involvement for Field‐Context and to Ensure Relevance of OutputsThe proactive inclusion of participants from three provinces in the workshop permitted separate assessments of influenza viruses in three different contexts by participants living in those contexts. This allowed nuanced RA and creation of risk management options specific to their epidemiological and cultural context. It emphasized both that not all risks are national, and that local knowledge is critical to assessment of context‐specific risks. Participants were able to then implement subsequent provincial assessments autonomously.3.1.5.Subsequent JRA Implementation in IndonesiaTo further support subnational JRAs, Indonesia initiated national JRA Training of Trainers (ToTs) activities in 2020 followed by ToTs in 10 provinces in 2021, which benefitted from the clear, stepwise guidance provided by the JRA‐OT. Subsequent JRAs applied the revised final tool and operational process and were conducted for SARS‐CoV‐2 virus (2021), Mycobacterium bovis (2022), avian influenza viruses (2022, 2023), rabies virus (2023), and Nipah virus (2026).3.2.United Republic of TanzaniaThe workshop in the United Republic of Tanzania, hereafter referred to as “Tanzania,” took place 1 year later, in Dar es Salaam on March 25–28, 2019. Tanzania was the first African country to conduct a JRA pilot workshop. Twenty‐four representatives of diverse government agencies, including disaster management, at central and subnational levels (e.g., Zanzibar), the One Health Coordination Desk (OHCD), and academic institutions participated during Days 1–3, whereas the JRA Secretariat, national facilitators, the One Health Coordinator, and the Minister of Health also attended Day 0 for the national facilitator training. Zoonotic influenza virus, Bacillus anthracis, and rabies virus were chosen as priority hazards. Both Tanzania's experience managing zoonotic diseases and the active OHCD for multisectoral coordination, which had experience organizing One Health trainings, facilitated success in pre‐pilot activities and workshop planning.The Tanzania pilot validated key findings from the Indon…

Because Indonesia was the first pilot, these lessons greatly impacted the JRA process and tool and all subsequent pilots.The Indonesia pilot generated key findings related to risk framing, pre‐workshop training, political will, and subnational involvement.3.1.1.Introducing a Risk‐Framing StepInitially, the draft JRA process did not include a step where decision‐makers could provide strategic and policy‐related inputs to frame the assessment. As such, Indonesian participants and facilitators found they had to identify the assessment's scope and policy objectives as a first step of the group work. This was time‐consuming and only possible because ministerial decision‐makers were present and engaged to advise. The national facilitators suggested that ministerial decision‐makers could undertake this step prior to the workshop, inspiring the addition of the pre‐pilot risk‐framing step to the final JRA.3.1.2.Adding a 1‐Day Pre‐Workshop Training for National FacilitatorsInitially, the “Day 0 national facilitators” training was also not part of the JRA process. Proactively, the Indonesian organizers initiated a full‐day pre‐pilot meeting of the JRA Secretariat and national technical staff to familiarize national facilitators with the JRA steps and to review the workshop objectives. These included staff from the provinces, and hereafter, the term “national facilitators” is inclusive of subnational staff. The entire team agreed that this pre‐pilot meeting was critical to the success of the workshop as it ensured that national facilitators (1) understood the JRA principles, step‐wise process, and tool; (2) practiced facilitation skills with support from the external facilitators prior to the workshop; and (3) could take a leading role in facilitation the next day. Skilled national facilitators would not only bring local context and perspectives but also create JRA sustainability, as external facilitators would no longer be needed for subsequent national and subnational JRAs. Subsequently, “Day 0” was incorporated for all future pilots, with national facilitators and JRA Secretariat attending Days 0–3 and all other participants attending Days 1–3. “Day 0” is not included in the tool as the JRA is meant to be done autonomously by countries, that is, once facilitators are familiar with the JRA tool and process.3.1.3.Importance of Political Will for JRA SuccessThe Government of Indonesia (GOI) was the first government to request a JRA workshop in 2017. The Ministry of Health (MoH), Ministry of Agriculture (MoA), and Coordinating Ministry of Human Development and Culture (Kemenko PMK) were strongly involved in planning and implementation. Director‐level representatives from these agencies were present during the entire workshop, contributed operationally to discussions, and were available to support the unanticipated risk‐framing activity. Not only did the Director General of MoH Prevention and Disease Control open the JRA, but he also requested a side meeting with the JRA Secretariat to show his direct support and appreciation of the JRA initiative and One Health approaches in general. The team agreed that this high‐level political engagement, as well as leveraging the strong national One Health culture, facilitated the later implementation of JRAs at national and subnational levels [10, 11]. The MoH proposed translating and adapting the tool further for the Indonesian context and embedding JRA within the national and provincial frameworks for zoonoses and other emerging infectious diseases based on the existing infrastructure and legal framework. This would be coordinated centrally by Kemenko PMK in collaboration with MoH, MoA, and Ministry of Environment and Forestry. Political will is now highlighted in the final JRA tool as a key element for enhancing the JRA success.3.1.4.Subnational Involvement for Field‐Context and to Ensure Relevance of OutputsThe proactive inclusion of participants from three provinces in the workshop permitted separate assessments of influenza viruses in three different contexts by participants living in those contexts. This allowed nuanced RA and creation of risk management options specific to their epidemiological and cultural context. It emphasized both that not all risks are national, and that local knowledge is critical to assessment of context‐specific risks. Participants were able to then implement subsequent provincial assessments autonomously.3.1.5.Subsequent JRA Implementation in IndonesiaTo further support subnational JRAs, Indonesia initiated national JRA Training of Trainers (ToTs) activities in 2020 followed by ToTs in 10 provinces in 2021, which benefitted from the clear, stepwise guidance provided by the JRA‐OT. Subsequent JRAs applied the revised final tool and operational process and were conducted for SARS‐CoV‐2 virus (2021), Mycobacterium bovis (2022), avian influenza viruses (2022, 2023), rabies virus (2023), and Nipah virus (2026).3.2.United Republic of TanzaniaThe workshop in the United Republic of Tanzania, hereafter referred to as “Tanzania,” took place 1 year later, in Dar es Salaam on March 25–28, 2019. Tanzania was the first African country to conduct a JRA pilot workshop. Twenty‐four representatives of diverse government agencies, including disaster management, at central and subnational levels (e.g., Zanzibar), the One Health Coordination Desk (OHCD), and academic institutions participated during Days 1–3, whereas the JRA Secretariat, national facilitators, the One Health Coordinator, and the Minister of Health also attended Day 0 for the national facilitator training. Zoonotic influenza virus, Bacillus anthracis, and rabies virus were chosen as priority hazards. Both Tanzania's experience managing zoonotic diseases and the active OHCD for multisectoral coordination, which had experience organizing One Health trainings, facilitated success in pre‐pilot activities and workshop planning.The Tanzania pilot validated key findings from the Indonesia pilot. As with Indonesia, Tanzanian participants suggested organizing nationally led ToT at the central and subnational levels. The importance of political will and high‐level input was affirmed, with ministerial participation on all 4 days of the workshop. Zanzibar was highlighted as a priority setting for implementing subnational JRAs, confirming their importance and value. Further findings included the use of virtual risk framing and using existing structures to sustain JRA implementation.3.2.1.Risk Framing Through Virtual ConsultationTanzania was one of the first countries to conduct a risk framing and the first done virtually with support from the JRA Secretariat. Practical lessons were learned about risk‐framing implementation, for example, that each hazard should be framed separately, and that the risk‐framing template should contain only information strictly necessary to focus the RA. Importantly, Tanzania demonstrated that the risk framing was effectively done virtually, and benefits of the virtual risk‐framing meeting were noted by the JRA Secretariat.3.2.2.Utilizing the Existing Multisectoral Coordination Mechanism as JRA Steering CommitteeAlready in 2015, Tanzania had developed and implemented its Prime Ministerial level One Health Strategic Plan and had establ…
full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionTo address the lack of One Health operational tools to guide joint, multisectoral RA for zoonotic disease threats, the Tripartite co‐developed the JRA‐OT with inputs from 15 pilot countries and international experts. Between 2015 and 2020, feedback was incorporated iteratively into the JRA‐OT by a Tripartite Secretariat to generate the final version [8] published in 2020.Pilots in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia were the first to be conducted in their respective geographical regions and generated key lessons that were particularly important for informing the final tool and, thus, were selected for detailed description in this manuscript. There was much overlap across the findings from these countries, suggesting that they also represented countries generally. Key findings included the (1) value of policy‐level risk framing, (2) importance of political will and leveraging existing One Health culture from the three countries, (3) need for subnational engagement, (4) inclusion of all relevant sectors, and (5) necessity of providing clear, stepwise operational guidance and ToTs (Table 3).TABLE 3Summary of key lessons learned or confirmed across pilots and integrated into the final Joint Risk Assessment (JRA) tool and process.Summary of key lessons learned or confirmed through JRA pilotsLesson learned inIndonesiaTanzaniaGeorgiaValue of policy‐level risk framing (in person or online)xxxImportance of political will and leveraging existing One Health culturexxxNeed for subnational engagementxxxImportance of including all relevant sectorsxNecessity of providing clear, stepwise operational guidance and training of trainersxx4.1.Value of Policy‐Level Risk FramingOne of the most important findings across pilots was the need for a formal risk‐framing process led by decision‐makers ahead of the workshop. In Indonesia, participants realized that defining the scope, objectives, and policy priorities during the workshop itself was inefficient and only possible because senior officials were present. Tanzania further demonstrated that risk framing could be conducted effectively through virtual consultations and highlighted the importance of framing each hazard separately. In Georgia, better aligning the hazards and framing with national priorities related to tourism and trade on Day 0 reinforced the importance of strong policy input in hazard selection and framing prior to the workshop.4.2.Importance of Political Will and Leveraging Existing One Health CultureAll three pilots showed that high‐level political commitment and existing multisectoral One Health coordination mechanisms were critical for successful implementation, as proposed by Yopa et al. [14]. Indonesia benefited from strong ministerial engagement and an established One Health governance structure, which later supported national and provincial JRA expansion. Tanzania's politically supported OHCD played a central role in organizing and sustaining JRA activities, whereas ministerial participation throughout the workshop reinforced national ownership. Similarly, Georgia's existing One Health Division within the NCDC facilitated planning, coordination, and policy relevance. Across pilots, political support increased participant engagement, improved alignment with national priorities, and facilitated translating JRA findings into action.4.3.Need for Subnational EngagementThe pilots consistently demonstrated that involving subnational participants improved the relevance and practicality of assessments. During pilots, subnational participants were noted to be especially engaged and motivated to act. In Indonesia, representatives from three provinces assessed influenza risks in their own local contexts, enabling development of tailored risk management strategies and demonstrating that zoonotic risks are often context‐specific rather than purely national. Tanzania identified Zanzibar as a priority setting for future subnational JRAs, highlighting the value of localized implementation. In Georgia, regional participants emphasized differences in rabies epidemiology across areas and proposed immediate use of JRA methods at the subnational level. Overall, the pilots showed that subnational participation strengthens contextual understanding, improves local ownership, and supports implementation of locally relevant mitigation measures.4.4.Inclusion of all Relevant SectorsAnother key lesson was the importance of ensuring representation from all relevant sectors in JRA workshops. Georgia particularly illustrated this challenge when the absence of the wildlife sector limited discussions on rabies risks involving wildlife transmission. This experience demonstrated that gaps in sectoral participation can reduce the completeness and quality of assessments. However, it also showed that the JRA process itself can help identify missing stakeholders and strengthen multisectoral collaboration over time. Across pilots, broad participation from human health, animal health, environment, disaster management, and other sectors was recognized as essential for comprehensive RA and effective One Health coordination for zoonotic diseases.4.5.Necessity of Clear, Stepwise Operational Guidance, and ToTsThe pilots highlighted the need for practical, stepwise operational guidance and strong national facilitation capacity. Indonesia pioneered the Day 0 national facilitator training, which became a standard feature of subsequent JRAs. This training helped facilitators understand the methodology, practice facilitation skills, and eventually lead workshops independently, reducing reliance on external experts. Pilots in Tanzania and Georgia validated the value of this approach, with national facilitators increasingly taking ownership of workshop implementation. The Georgia pilot highlighted the need for clearer guidance on hazard selection and joint risk‐framing procedures that were then added into the tool. In both Indonesia and Tanzania, participants recommended national and subnational ToT programs to build sustainable in‐country expertise. Together, these experiences emphasized that successful JRA implementation depends not only on the tool itself, but also on clear, stepwise operational guidance, standardized processes, and national capacity building.After review and discussion of these key lessons learned, the JRA Secretariat made the following revisions to the JRA tool and process: (1) introduction of a dedicated pre‐workshop risk‐framing Step 2 in the JRA process, led by decision‐makers, including a template for framing risks related to each hazard identified in Step 1; (2) highlighting the importance of political will and the opportunity to leverage existing national One Health structures to sustainably implement JRA; and (3) highlighting the importance of prospective inclusion of all relevant sectors, with participation of national and subnational levels, especially relevant in Step 3 where participants are being identified. The full‐day training for national facilitators on Day 0 was added to planning for all future workshops to foster ownership in country pilots, familiarize national facilitators, including subnational staff, with the JRA steps and some basic facilitation principles and review the workshop objectives.All three countries saw the JRA as an opportunity to operationalize One Health strategies while producing practical, tangible outputs, specifically, consolidated hazard information, qualitative risk estimates, and options for risk‐based management and communication.The evidence‐based JRA output served as advocacy to secure high‐level commitment and resources for risk mitigation. Participants from different sectors often still did not know each other, despite ongoing multisectoral activities and high levels of One Health awareness further emphasized the need to strengthen routine collaborative activities, such as JRA.The JRA process can present challenges. full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionKnowledge iteratively gained during pilots was critical to enhance the usefulness and effectiveness of the JRA process and tool, and ownership by different sectors. Key lessons can be grouped into the following categories: The value of policy‐level risk framingThe importance of political will and leveraging existing One Health structuresThe need for subnational engagementThe importance of all relevant sectors being engaged and presentThe need for clear, stepwise guidance to facilitate efficient collaboration and support training of national trainersThe JRA pilots demonstrated that effective zoonotic disease RA requires strong integration of technical analysis with policy‐level decision‐making, particularly through early and structured risk framing. Sustained political commitment and established One Health coordination mechanisms were critical enablers of successful JRA implementation and long‐term national ownership. Inclusion of subnational actors and all relevant sectors significantly improved the contextual relevance, completeness, and operational value of RAs.The pilots showed that JRAs can serve not only as technical tools for RA, but also as mechanisms for strengthening multisectoral collaboration, information sharing, and One Health governance. Standardized operational guidance, facilitator training, and nationally led ToTs were essential for building sustainable country capacity and reducing reliance on external support.The JRA was co‐developed iteratively and inclusively across countries, sectors, and scales to meet objectives laid down by national governments and experts in RA and zoonotic diseases to assess risks, and thus models One Health best practice in both content and process and ensures ownership by the different sectors. The methodology can be used as a model for development of other multisectoral operational processes and tools. The JRA's inclusive, systematic, and evidence‐based RA process is now available to all countries, improving management of critical national zoonotic disease risks.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionActions and policies to identify, assess, manage, and reduce risks from zoonotic diseases benefit from functional collaboration and engagement across stakeholders and sectors, including academia, the private sector, local communities, and government ministries responsible for human health, animal health, food safety, wildlife, environment, trade, education, security and disasters, and the economy [1]. Under the International Health Regulations (2005) monitoring and evaluation framework—Joint External Evaluation guidance [2], countries should have the capacity to conduct joint assessments of risk for zoonotic diseases using a One Health approach.In 2014, countries concerned about the potential spread of a zoonotic avian influenza A(H7N9) virus strain in Asia wished to align the results of sectoral risk assessments (RAs) and risk‐related communication messages but encountered challenges in sharing information and conducting RA jointly across sectors. Due to its sensitive nature, information related to zoonotic diseases can potentially influence consumer behavior and/or compromise a country's economy or tourism if made public. Sharing such information between sectors often must be authorized and may be restricted or delayed, especially in the absence of clear sharing mechanisms or policies. Further, although countries could access sector‐specific RA methodologies and processes, they encountered challenges in assessing risks jointly when encountering differing steps and terminology across RA methods and the reluctance of sectors to agree on an approach unfamiliar to them in the absence of expert guidance. These countries requested assistance from the Tripartite [3] to identify and propose a technically sound approach to conducting joint, multisectoral zoonotic disease RA.Technical aspects of estimating risks are, in principle, similar across RA methods, and it is normally possible to incorporate information from other sectors during sector‐specific zoonotic disease RAs. However, each sector‐specific method evolved to achieve different objectives. Consequently, RA methods are operationally different, do not easily align, and do not lend themselves to joint use. Although many institutions and agencies publish RA reports for zoonotic diseases, an extensive search of published guidance for conducting zoonotic disease RA across health‐related disciplines identified only sector‐specific tools available at that time. Further, the guidance from WHO [4], WOAH [5](updated in 2024) and FAO [6](available internally but unpublished at the time) referred to assessment for zoonotic diseases but had been developed exclusively by and for the human health and animal health sectors, respectively. The RA procedures of the Codex Alimentarius Commission [7] were also available but primarily focused on quantitative assessment of contaminants in food and were not practical for use by countries. To fill this gap, the Tripartite convened international RA experts and pilot countries to iteratively co‐develop the first‐ever One Health operational tool for conducting zoonotic disease RA jointly across sectors.The Joint Risk Assessment (JRA) was published as the Joint Risk Assessment Operational Tool (JRA‐OT) in 2020 [8], as one of the operational tools supporting the Tripartite Zoonoses Guide [1]. The JRA‐OT provides a systematic and iterative step‐by‐step process to bring together stakeholders from different sectors. Together, they share expertise, discuss available information, and jointly identify and qualitatively assess risks associated with zoonotic hazards nationally and subnationally, based on strategic policy concerns. Benefits include the following: Facilitates sharing of information and expertise from all relevant sectors, increasing the technical validity of results, including evidence‐based management measures and communication messages.Facilitates agreement and ownership of results across sectors, allowing development of nuanced and acceptable management interventions with fewer negative externalities.Prospectively considers strategic policy needs across sectors at national and subnational levels, expediting aligned and contextualized implementation done jointly or separately by each sector.Fosters mutual understanding of perceptions, mandates, constraints, and daily work across sectors, improving communication for future collaborative activities, including emergency response.Identifies missing information, allowing targeting of surveillance, research, and capacity building.Facilitates political engagement and support for sustained One Health collaboration through establishment of a routine technical, output‐driven collaborative process located within a multisectoral coordination and governance infrastructure.This article describes the iterative and collaborative process undertaken to co‐develop the JRA, which is an example of and a model for applied One Health, demonstrating: Initiation based on needs of the user communityBalanced, shared leadership across multiple sectorsInclusion of expertise, perspectives, information, and experiences from across a broad, inclusive, and multi‐scalar scope of technical and policy stakeholdersIterative consideration and integration of knowledge insights acquired during implementationThe JRA itself exemplifies best practices in One Health implementation, namely, Developing a shared objectiveUsing a standardized process to facilitate collaboration, reduce conflict, and achieve joint outputsProviding tangible outputs, specifically, consolidated hazard information, qualitative risk estimates, and options for risk‐based management and communication, that are immediately practical, relevant to local contexts, and useful for diverse stakeholdersBuilding technical capacityDemonstrating transparency and inclusivityPromoting trust, awareness, and relationship‐building across sectors and scalesHere we describe national pilots in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia, selected on the basis of their importance in informing the final JRA process and tool. Our findings serve as a model to inform co‐development of other multisectoral operational tools by applying an inclusive and consultative process consistent with the One Health approach. 2.1.Initial Tool DevelopmentThe JRA‐OT development began in 2014 and was led by a multisectoral international team of epidemiologists, zoonotic disease experts, and RA experts from six countries in three regions, including many from this team of authors, convened through virtual meetings. elements_en.study_design_and_population: The 64 participants included representatives from central government ministries spanning human and animal health, forestry and environment, security and disasters, the Coordinating Ministry of Human Development and Culture, and health and livestock disease investigation staff from three provinces.
elements_en.methods: Under the International Health Regulations (2005) monitoring and evaluation framework—Joint External Evaluation guidance [2], countries should have the capacity to conduct joint assessments of risk for zoonotic diseases using a One Health approach.In 2014, countries concerned about the potential spread of a zoonotic avian influenza A(H7N9) virus strain in Asia wished to align the results of sectoral risk assessments (RAs) and risk‐related communication messages but encountered challenges in sharing information and conducting RA jointly across sectors.
elements_en.main_results: In Georgia, better aligning the hazards and framing with national priorities related to tourism and trade on Day 0 reinforced the importance of strong policy input in hazard selection and framing prior to the workshop.4.2.Importance of Political Will and Leveraging Existing One Health CultureAll three pilots showed that high‐level political commitment and existing multisectoral One Health coordination mechanisms were critical for successful implementation, as proposed by Yopa et al.
elements_en.interpretation_and_novelty: Key lessons can be grouped into the following categories: The value of policy‐level risk framingThe importance of political will and leveraging existing One Health structuresThe need for subnational engagementThe importance of all relevant sectors being engaged and presentThe need for clear, stepwise guidance to facilitate efficient collaboration and support training of national trainersThe JRA pilots demonstrated that effective zoonotic disease RA requires strong integration of technical analysis with policy‐level decision‐making, particularly through early and structured risk framing.
elements_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The process serves as a model for co‐development of other multisectoral operational tools.Keywords: Joint Operational Tools, One Health, risk assessment, zoonoses Piloting of the Tripartite Joint Risk Assessment (JRA) process and tool in countries provided feedback for improvement, evidence‐based estimates of national risks from priority zoonotic diseases, and practical training of national facilitators.
elements_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The methodology can be used as a model for development of other multisectoral operational processes and tools.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 4. 讨论:为了解决缺乏指导联合、多部门风险评估的One Health操作工具的问题,三方共同开发了JRA-OT工具,结合了15个试点国家和国际专家的意见。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 64名参与者包括来自中央政府各部委的代表,涵盖人类和动物健康、林业与环境、安全与灾害等领域,以及来自三个省份的人类健康和牲畜疾病调查工作人员。
elements_zh.methods: 根据《国际卫生条例(2005)》的监测与评估框架——联合外部评估指南[2],各国应具备使用One Health方法进行人兽共患病风险联合评估的能力。2014年,一些关注亚洲地区可能传播的禽流感A(H7N9)病毒的国家希望协调部门风险评估(RA)结果和相关风险信息传播,但在跨部门共享信息和联合进行风险评估方面遇到了挑战。
elements_zh.main_results: 在格鲁吉亚,Day 0时更好地将危害与旅游业和贸易等国家优先事项对齐,强化了在研讨会前进行危害选择和框架构建时,强有力的政策输入的重要性。4.2. 政治意愿的重要性及利用现有的One Health文化:所有三个试点都表明,高层政治承诺和现有的多部门One Health协调机制对于成功实施至关重要,正如Yopa等人所提出的。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 关键经验可以分为以下几类:政策层面风险框架的价值;政治意愿的重要性及利用现有的One Health结构;次国家层面参与的必要性;所有相关部门参与和出席的重要性;为促进高效协作并支持国家培训师的培训,需要清晰、分步骤的指导;JRA试点表明,有效的风险评估需要技术分析与政策层面决策的强整合,特别是在早期和结构化的风险框架构建过程中。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 该流程为其他多部门操作工具的共同开发提供了一个模型。关键词:联合操作工具、One Health、风险评估、人兽共患病。在各国开展三方联合风险评估(JRA)流程和工具的试点,提供了改进反馈、基于证据的国家优先人兽共患病风险估计以及国家协调员的实用培训。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该方法可以作为开发其他多部门操作流程和工具的模型。

papers.title_zh: 通过在印度尼西亚、坦桑尼亚联合共和国和格鲁吉亚开展试点,迭代开发三方联合风险评估操作流程和工具:整合来自试点国家的信息
papers.source_body_en: Development criteria included a standard, systematic, qualitative, and multisectoral RA process, facilitating incorporation of expert opinion and sector‐specific RA results. Key findings included the (1) value of policy‐level risk framing, (2) importance of political will, (3) need for subnational engagement, (4) importance of including all relevant sectors, and (5) necessity of clear, stepwise guidance to facilitate efficient collaboration and support training of national trainers.ConclusionsCo‐development of the JRA using country pilots and expert consultations allowed for field‐testing and iterative improvement of the tool, ensuring incorporation of user requirements, robust methodology for the joint, multisectoral assessment of national zoonotic disease risks, and ownership by the different sectors. They reviewed and examined existing sector‐specific RA methods and tools for their suitability and relevance and agreed on the following criteria for the joint RA: Provide a standard, systematic process for conducting evidence‐based RA on joint priority zoonotic disease hazards.Be qualitative and facilitate incorporation of expert opinion when only minimal and/or poor‐quality data are available.Allow identification of data gaps, and benefit from iterative use as additional data becomes available.Promote use of data and results from sector‐specific RAs.Provide step‐by‐step operational guidance to facilitate effective and equitable collaboration and sharing of information, expertise, and perspectives.Be prospectively joint across all relevant sectors, that is, public health (e.g., ministries of health, public health agencies), animal health (e.g., veterinary services), environmental (e.g., wildlife health, environmental protection agencies), and others, such as security a...
papers.abstract_zh: 开发标准、系统、定性且多部门的风险评估(RA)流程,有助于纳入专家意见和部门特定的风险评估结果。关键发现包括:(1)政策层面的风险框架的价值;(2)政治意愿的重要性;(3)需要进行次国家层面的参与;(4)纳入所有相关部门的重要性;(5)需要清晰、分步骤的指导,以促进高效协作并支持国家培训师的培训。结论:通过国家试点和专家咨询共同开发联合风险评估(JRA)工具,使得该工具能够在实地进行测试并进行迭代改进,确保纳入用户需求、建立联合、多部门评估国家人兽共患病风险的稳健方法,并实现不同部门的拥有感。他们审查并评估了现有部门特定的风险评估方法和工具,以确定其适用性和相关性,并就联合风险评估达成了以下标准:提供一个标准、系统的过程,用于基于证据的联合优先人兽共患病危害风险评估。应为定性,并在仅有少量和/或低质量数据时,促进纳入专家意见。应能够识别数据缺口,并在获得额外数据时通过迭代使用获益。应促进使用部门特定风险评估的数据和结果。应提供分步骤的操作指导,以促进有效且公平的协作,以及信息、专业知识和观点的共享。应前瞻性地联合所有相关部门,即公共卫生(例如卫生部、公共卫生机构)、动物健康(例如兽医服务)、环境(例如野生动物健康、环境保护机构)等,以及其他部门,如安全和灾害等。

12 October 2026 • Big Picture Nipah virus explained: How it spreads and how Bangladesh can stay safe Published : 29 January 2026 • Updated : 29 January 2026, 16:28 • HEALTH & FITNESS SHARE A Ayman Anika Ayman Anika Photo: Collected / gabby k / Pexels For many of us, the word “Nipah” is not abstract. It carries memories of quarantined villages, restricted movement, and anxious nights spent waiting for test results. With new Nipah cases reported in neighbouring India, and airports across Asia stepping up screening, the concern feels immediate — not distant. Nipah virus is not new to Bangladesh. Since the first recorded outbreak in 2001, the country has seen repeated cases almost every year, particularly in winter. Unlike many infectious diseases that arrive from elsewhere, Nipah is already part of our ecological reality. Tap here to add The Daily Star as a trusted source How Nipah spreads Fruit bats are the natural carriers of the Nipah virus. In Bangladesh, transmission to humans most commonly occurs through raw date palm sap contaminated by bat saliva or urine. The practice of drinking fresh, unprocessed sap remains one of the biggest risk factors. The virus can also spread by eating fruits partially eaten or contaminated by bats, through close contact with infected animals, and from human to human via bodily fluids such as saliva, respiratory droplets, blood, or urine. Several outbreaks in Bangladesh have shown clear evidence of person-to-person transmission, especially among family members and caregivers. This makes Nipah particularly dangerous in household and hospital settings where close contact is unavoidable. Symptoms that should not be ignored Nipah infection does not always start dramatically. Early symptoms often include fever, headache, muscle pain, sore throat, and fatigue — signs that can easily be mistaken for flu or viral fever. In more severe cases, the virus attacks the brain, leading to encephalitis. Symptoms may escalate quickly to dizziness, confusion, seizures, difficulty breathing, and loss of consciousness. The disease can progress within days. Fatality rates reported in South Asia range between 40 and 75 per cent. Survivors may suffer long-term neurological complications, including memory loss, personality changes, and difficulty concentrating. There is no specific antiviral treatment and no approved vaccine. Medical care focuses on supportive treatment, which makes early detection critical. Why this matters right now Recent cases in India, particularly in West Bengal, are geographically close to Bangladesh. While Nipah does not spread easily through casual contact or air travel, authorities have increased airport screening as a precaution. These steps are meant to detect symptoms early, not to signal widespread danger. For Bangladesh, the bigger challenge lies at home. Rural awareness remains uneven, and seasonal behaviours — especially consuming raw date palm sap — continue despite years of warnings. What prevention actually looks like Preventing Nipah does not require drastic lifestyle changes, but it does require consistency. Avoiding raw or fermented date palm sap is one of the most effective measures. Fruits should be washed thoroughly and not eaten if visibly bitten or damaged. People should avoid close contact with sick animals and seek medical attention if they develop a fever after possible exposure. Caregivers should use protective measures when looking after suspected patients, especially in home settings. Nipah is not a virus that spreads silently across cities. It spreads through habits, proximity, and delayed response. For us, vigilance is not about panic. It is about recognising a familiar threat, understanding how it moves, and choosing prevention over regret. For all latest news, follow The Daily Star's Google News channel. analysis.brief_en: The article explains the Nipah virus, emphasizing its transmission routes and the importance of prevention in Bangladesh. The Nipah virus is not new to the country, with repeated cases almost every year, particularly in winter. It is primarily spread through raw date palm sap contaminated by bat saliva or urine, and can also spread through close contact with infected animals or via bodily fluids in human-to-human transmission. Symptoms include fever, headache, muscle pain, and can escalate to encephalitis, with fatality rates ranging between 40 and 75 per cent in South Asia. Survivors may face long-term neurological issues. The article highlights that while Nipah does not spread easily through casual contact or air travel, authorities have increased airport screening as a precaution. Prevention measures include avoiding raw or fermented date palm sap, washing fruits thoroughly, and seeking medical attention after possible exposure. The focus is on awareness and consistent prevention rather than panic.

Web Desk February 09, 2026 The World Health Organization said that a woman in northern Bangladesh died in January after being infected with the Nipah virus. Bangladesh reports cases of the virus almost every year, and this latest case comes after two infections were recently detected in neighboring India, leading several Asian countries to increase health screenings at airports. According to the WHO, the woman, who was between 40 and 50 years old, developed symptoms on January 21, including fever and headache, followed by excessive salivation, confusion, and seizures. She died a week later, and the infection was confirmed the following day. The patient had no recent travel history but had consumed raw date palm sap, which is considered a possible source of infection. Health officials monitored 35 people who had contact with her, and all tested negative, with no additional cases reported so far. Nipah virus usually spreads through food or fruit contaminated by infected bats. The infection can be fatal in up to 75 percent of cases, but it does not spread easily from person to person. After India reported cases in West Bengal, countries including Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Pakistan introduced temperature screening at airports as a precaution. The WHO stated that the risk of international spread remains low and that no travel or trade restrictions are currently recommended. In 2025, Bangladesh reported four laboratory-confirmed deaths caused by the Nipah virus. Web Desk February 09, 2026 The World Health Organization said that a woman in northern Bangladesh died in January after being infected with the Nipah virus. Bangladesh reports cases of the virus almost every year, and this latest case comes after two infections were recently detected in neighboring India, leading several Asian countries to increase health screenings at airports. According to the WHO, the woman, who was between 40 and 50 years old, developed symptoms on January 21, including fever and headache, followed by excessive salivation, confusion, and seizures. She died a week later, and the infection was confirmed the following day. The patient had no recent travel history but had consumed raw date palm sap, which is considered a possible source of infection. Health officials monitored 35 people who had contact with her, and all tested negative, with no additional cases reported so far. Nipah virus usually spreads through food or fruit contaminated by infected bats. The infection can be fatal in up to 75 percent of cases, but it does not spread easily from person to person. After India reported cases in West Bengal, countries including Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Pakistan introduced temperature screening at airports as a precaution. The WHO stated that the risk of international spread remains low and that no travel or trade restrictions are currently recommended. In 2025, Bangladesh reported four laboratory-confirmed deaths caused by the Nipah virus. Testing of the drug is scheduled to begin in April in Belgium, according to zakon.kz. The University of Tokyo's Center for Advanced Science and Technology is developing the vaccine. The need for the drug stems from recent outbreaks of the disease in India, which began in January of this year. The Nipah virus is a zoonotic infection transmitted from animals to humans. Large fruit bats are the natural reservoir for the infection. The disease is highly fatal and can cause severe damage to the nervous and respiratory systems. There is currently no approved effective vaccine against this virus worldwide. If trials are successful, this new development could help prevent future outbreaks and reduce epidemiological risks. news.title_zh: 疫苗 与 尼帕病毒 的临床试验将在日本开始 - Turkmenportal.com
news.source_body_en: Clinical trials of a vaccine against the Nipah virus are set to begin in Japan, as announced by the University of Tokyo's Center for Advanced Science and Technology. The trials are scheduled to start in April in Belgium, driven by recent outbreaks of the virus in India, which began in January 2026. The Nipah virus, a zoonotic infection transmitted from animals to humans, primarily through large fruit bats, is highly fatal and can cause severe damage to the nervous and respiratory systems. Currently, there is no approved effective vaccine against this virus globally, making the development of a new vaccine critical for preventing future outbreaks and reducing epidemiological risks. The trials represent a significant step in addressing the threat posed by the Nipah virus, which has been a concern due to its high fatality rate and potential for severe health impacts.
news.content_zh: 针对尼帕病毒的疫苗临床试验即将在日本开始,正如东京大学先进科学技术中心所宣布的。试验计划于2026年4月在比利时启动,这是由于近期印度出现的暴发,该暴发始于2026年1月。尼帕病毒是一种从动物传播给人类的人兽共患病,主要通过大型果蝠传播,具有高度致命性,可对神经系统和呼吸系统造成严重损害。目前,全球尚无批准有效的疫苗用于治疗该病毒,因此开发新的疫苗对于预防未来的暴发和降低流行病学风险至关重要。这些试验代表了应对尼帕病毒威胁的重要一步,该病毒因其高死亡率和可能对健康造成严重影响而备受关注。
news.summary_zh: 针对尼帕病毒的疫苗临床试验即将在日本开始,正如东京大学先进科学技术中心所宣布的。试验计划于2026年4月在比利时启动,这是由于近期印度出现的暴发,该暴发始于2026年1月。尼帕病毒是一种从动物传播给人类的人兽共患病,主要通过大型果蝠传播,具有高度致命性,可对神经系统和呼吸系统造成严重损害。目前,全球尚无批准有效的疫苗用于治疗该病毒,因此开发新的疫苗对于预防未来的暴发和降低流行病学风险至关重要。这些试验代表了应对尼帕病毒威胁的重要一步,该病毒因其高死亡率和可能对健康造成严重影响而备受关注。

news.content: Add ANI As A Trusted Source For Reliable Information Tue, Oct 13, 2026 |Updated 10:16 IST Toggle navigation Toggle navigation National General News Politics Features Business Entertainment Bollywood Hollywood Music Out of box Sports Cricket Football Others Tennis Hockey World Asia US Europe Pacific Others Middle East Health Tech Mobile Internet Science Others Videos National World Entertainment Sports Business Toggle navigation All you need to know about Nipah virus outbreak in Kerala Updated:3 years ago Kozhikode (Kerala), September 18 (ANI): Giving a significant update on the current situation of the Nipah Virus in Kerala and the state’s response to the virus outbreak, Kerala Health Minister Veena George said that ICMR and WHO had conducted studies on the issue and it was found that 9 states in India have the probability of Nipah occurrence and Kerala is one among them. She further said, “Also after 2018, we conducted surveillance and we found that the source of Nipah infection is bats. The virus we found in Kerala is identified as Indian Genotype or I Genotype which is similar to the strain found in Bangladesh. We have two strains of Nipah Virus one is Malaysian and the other from Bangladesh." The Health Minister's update underscores the government's commitment to swiftly and comprehensively address the Nipah virus situation in Kerala. Authorities are leaving no stone unturned in their efforts to contain the outbreak, trace contacts, and gather critical scientific data for a more informed response. Public health remains the top priority as the state works diligently to manage this health challenge. She also mentioned that the source of Nipah infection is bats, based on surveillance conducted after 2018. The update highlights that 9 states in India have the probability of Nipah occurrence, with Kerala being one of them. Authorities are actively working to contain the outbreak, trace contacts, and gather critical scientific data for a more informed response. The government has emphasized the importance of public health and is committed to managing this challenge effectively. The information is current as of the publication date on October 7, 2026, and the report underscores the ongoing efforts to address the situation.
news.content_zh: 印度喀拉拉邦的尼帕病毒 暴发引发了州政府的重大反应。2026年9月18日,喀拉拉邦卫生部长维娜·乔治表示,该州发现的病毒是印度基因型或I型基因型,与孟加拉国的毒株相似。她还提到,尼帕病毒感染的来源是蝙蝠,这是2018年后进行的监测得出的结论。更新指出,印度有9个州存在尼帕病毒出现的可能性,喀拉拉邦是其中之一。当局正在积极努力控制暴发,追踪接触者,并收集关键的科学数据以做出更明智的应对。政府强调了公共卫生的重要性,并致力于有效管理这一挑战。信息截至2026年10月7日的出版日期,报告强调了应对这一情况的持续努力。

protein,RBP)和融合蛋白(fu 瑞孚迪自动化解决方案>> 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 Open access 尼帕病毒(Nipah virus,NiV)是一种生物安全四级(biosafety level 4,BSL-4)病原体,持续对公共卫生构成重大威胁。病毒表面的两种包膜蛋白——受体结合蛋白(receptor-binding protein,RBP)和融合蛋白(fusion protein,F)——是中和抗体的主要靶点。然而,针对单一病毒抗原的抗体常导致耐药株的出现。本研究通过筛选噬菌体展示文库(phage display library),研究人员获得了一种靶向RBP头部结构域的C型纳米抗体(C-Nab),命名为G-3-1。半衰期延长的G-3-1-HLE(half-life-extended G-3-1-HLE)可有效保护仓鼠免受真实NiV攻击。此外,研究人员通过刚性(AP)12连接子将G-3-1与靶向F蛋白的纳米抗体2A1-3-8连接,构建了融合蛋白2A1-3-8-(AP)12-G-3-1。该融合蛋白展现出改善且更为平衡的中和活性。另外,2A1-3-8-(AP)12-G-3-1的体内预防功效在NiV假病毒(pseudovirus)感染的小鼠模型中得以验证。综上所述,这项关于双包膜蛋白靶向双特异性抗体的研究不仅提供了有前景的抗病毒候选分子,也为下一代抗体优化提供了重要的设计策略。 **论文解读:靶向双重包膜糖蛋白的双特异性纳米抗体有效中和尼帕病毒** 瑞孚迪多肽药物研发解决方案>>领 取 **研究背景与存在问题:** 尼帕病毒(Nipah virus,NiV)被世界卫生组织列为优先病原体,其病死率高达40%–75%,宿主范围广,且缺乏特异性治疗药物。2026年初,印度和孟加拉国再次暴发NiV疫情,并出现医护人员感染和死亡案例,凸显其作为“国际关注的突发公共卫生事件”的现实威胁。NiV分为马来西亚株(NiVM)和孟加拉株(NiVB),后者在人群中的病死率更高,且已证实存在人际传播。目前尚无获批用于人类的NiV疫苗或药物。病毒表面的受体结合蛋白(receptor-binding protein,RBP)和融合蛋白(fusion protein,F)是中和抗体的主要靶点,但针对单一抗原的抗体长期使用易诱发病毒逃逸突变,导致耐药株出现。既往的抗体组合或双特异性抗体策略多仅靶向RBP或F蛋白,且已有双特异性抗体DS90-m102.4在仓鼠模型中未能表现出超越单抗的保护效果,提示该策略仍有优化空间。 **研究内容与意义:** 研究人员通过筛选C型纳米抗体(C-Nab)噬菌体展示文库,获得靶向RBP头部结构域的亲本克隆G-0,并经三轮亲和力成熟得到高亲和力克隆G-3-1。将G-3-1与血清白蛋白靶向纳米抗体NbAlb1融合构建半衰期延长型抗体G-3-1-HLE,在仓鼠模型中证实其可提供50%的治疗性保护。进一步通过连接子类型、长度和串联方向的系统优化,研究人员构建了同时靶向F蛋白和RBP的双特异性纳米抗体2A1-3-8-(AP)12-G-3-1,该抗体在体外表现出增强且更为平衡的中和活性,并在小鼠NiV假病毒感染模型中展现出良好的预防保护效果。该研究不仅提供了应对NiV疫情的下一代抗体候选分子,也为双抗原靶向双特异性抗体的设计提供了重要策略。 **关键技术方法:** 研究人员使用来自中国典型培养物保藏中心的Vero、Vero E6、293T细胞,以及HEK293F细胞;NiVM、NiVB和亨德拉病毒(HeV)毒株来自中国科学院武汉病毒研究所国家病毒资源库。主要方法包括:基于噬菌体展示文库的生物淘选与亲和力成熟(error-prone PCR引入随机突变)、酶联免疫吸附试验(ELISA)和生物层干涉法(BLI)测定结合活性、基于VSV载体的假病毒中和试验、BSL-4设施内的真病毒空斑减少中和试验、冷冻电镜(cryo-EM)和AlphaFold 3结构预测、竞争ELISA和丙氨酸扫描突变进行表位鉴定、叙利亚金仓鼠药代动力学及攻毒治疗研究、BALB/c小鼠假病毒感染模型及抗体预防实验。 **研究结果:** **一、靶向RBP的C-Nab的鉴定。** 研究人员以NiVM-RBP头部结构域为抗原筛选C-Nab噬菌体展示文库,获得亲本克隆G-0。通过连续三轮针对NiVM-RBP、NiVB-RBP和HeV-RBP的亲和力成熟,筛选出优势克隆G-3-1。与G-0相比,G-3-1与HNV-RBP的结合活性显著增强,其中对HeV-RBP的结合提高超过500倍。BLI测定其与NiVM-RBP、NiVB-RBP和HeV-RBP的平衡解离常数(KD)分别为0.022 nM、0.250 nM和0.152 nM。在假病毒中和试验中,G-3-1对NiVM和HeV的中和活性较G-0分别提高189倍和650倍;对真实NiVM和NiVB的半数抑制浓度(IC50)分别为2.16 nM和3.58 nM。 **二、半衰期延长的G-3-1-HLE有效保护仓鼠抵抗NiV感染。** 由于纳米抗体分子量小(约15 kDa),体内清除快,研究人员将血清白蛋白靶向纳米抗体NbAlb1融合至G-3-1的C端,构建半衰期延长型抗体G-3-1-HLE。药代动力学分析显示,G-3-1-HLE在仓鼠体内的半衰期(t1/2)为36小时,较G-3-1(1.3小时)延长27.7倍,且生物利用度、清除率、平均驻留时间等参数均获改善。在1000 LD50 NiVM腹腔攻毒模型中,感染后2小时、1天和3天给予20 mg/kg G-3-1-HLE,可提供50%的治疗性保护,存活仓鼠体重呈持续上升趋势。 **三、G-3-1靶向RBP头部结构域上的受体结合域。** 研究人员通过cryo-EM获得NiVM-RBP头部/G-3-1复合物约10 ?分辨率的低分辨率三维结构,显示G-3-1以近似垂直于RBP表面的方向结合。AlphaFold 3预测的复合物模型与三维结构相符,预测埋藏面积为1315.8 ?2,Loop 3贡献最大。竞争ELISA证明G-3-1与Ephrin B2和m102.4(靶向RBD的抗体)完全竞争结合RBP,而与靶向非RBD表位的HENV-32、nAH1.3和hAH1.3无竞争。丙氨酸扫描突变实验表明,NiVM-RBP中F458和G506残基对其结合敏感,HeV-RBP中敏感残基更多,该差异可能与其NiV偏向的中和活性有关。综合结果表明G-3-1的表位位于RBP头部的受体结合域(RBD),其机制是阻断RBP与Ephrin B2受体的结合。 **四、RBP和F靶向C-Nab的串联融合增强中和广度和效力。** 研究人员利用刚性(AP)12连接子将靶向RBP的G-3-1与靶向F蛋白的C-Nab 2A1-3-8串联,构建双特异性纳米抗体2A1-3-8-(AP)12-G-3-1。在连接子优化过程中,刚性连接子(EAAAK)n和(AP)n优于柔性连接子(G4S)n,且2A1-3-8位于N端、G-3-1位于C端的长刚性连接子(AP)12效果最佳。与单克隆抗体2A1-3-8和G-3-1相比,2A1-3-8-(AP)12-G-3-1对NiVM、NiVB和HeV的中和活性表现出更高效力和更均衡的特征,其对NiVM和NiVB的活性较2A1-3-8分别提高1.3倍和6.0倍,较G-3-1分别提高11.5倍、18.7倍和1015.8倍。 **五、2A1-3-8-(AP)12-G-3-1有效预防小鼠NiV假病毒感染。** 研究人员建立了一种基于生物发光成像的BALB/c小鼠NiV假病毒感染模型,确定假病毒主要靶向脾脏,肺部和肝脏有较弱信号。预防实验中,在假病毒攻击前30分钟腹腔注射25 mg/kg抗体,结果显示所有抗体处理组(2A1-3-8、G-3-1、2A1-3-8-(AP)12-G-3-1和m102.4)均显著降低了脾脏、肺和肝脏中的病毒载量。2A1-3-8-(AP)12-G-3-1展现出色的预防活性,但在本实验剂量下未表现出显著优于单个C-Nab的保护效力。 **讨论与结论:** 讨论部分指出,纳米抗体具有组织穿透力强(如穿越血脑屏障)、生产成本低、可识别隐蔽表位等优势,但体内清除快是其主要限制。G-3-1-HLE仅提供50%保护,可能与其本身中和活性不够强或半衰期仍相对有限有关。RBD是NiV RBP上的免疫优势表位,针对RBD的抗体最为丰富且高效。鉴于单靶点抗体的逃逸风险,同时靶向RBP和F蛋白的双特异性抗体策略具有重要意义。连接子的选择对双特异性抗体功能至关重要,本研究通过系统优化确定了最佳连接子。双特异性抗体可能通过同时结合同一病毒颗粒上的两种包膜蛋白,或交联不同病毒颗粒发挥中和作用,但具体机制仍需进一步验证。研究局限性包括:未在真实病毒模型中进行剂量滴定和预防/治疗效果的全面评估、未对双特异性抗体抗逃逸突变能力进行直接验证。结论部分指出,该双特异性纳米抗体2A1-3-8-(AP)12-G-3-1不仅具有强效且平衡的NiV和HeV中和活性,还在小鼠模型中提供了有效的假病毒预防保护,为应对未来NiV暴发提供了有前景的候选分子,并为下一代双抗原靶向双特异性抗体的设计提供了宝贵策略。 nM、0.250 nM和0.152 nM。在假病毒中和试验中,G-3-1对NiVM和HeV的中和活性较G-0分别提高189倍和650倍;对真实NiVM和NiVB的半数抑制浓度(IC50)分别为2.16 nM和3.58 nM。 **二、半衰期延长的G-3-1-HLE有效保护仓鼠抵抗NiV感染。** 由于纳米抗体分子量小(约15 kDa),体内清除快,研究人员将血清白蛋白靶向纳米抗体NbAlb1融合至G-3-1的C端,构建半衰期延长型抗体G-3-1-HLE。药代动力学分析显示,G-3-1-HLE在仓鼠体内的半衰期(t1/2)为36小时,较G-3-1(1.3小时)延长27.7倍,且生物利用度、清除率、平均驻留时间等参数均获改善。在1000 LD50 NiVM腹腔攻毒模型中,感染后2小时、1天和3天给予20 mg/kg G-3-1-HLE,可提供50%的治疗性保护,存活仓鼠体重呈持续上升趋势。 **三、G-3-1靶向RBP头部结构域上的受体结合域。** 研究人员通过cryo-EM获得NiVM-RBP头部/G-3-1复合物约10 ?分辨率的低分辨率三维结构,显示G-3-1以近似垂直于RBP表面的方向结合。AlphaFold 3预测的复合物模型与三维结构相符,预测埋藏面积为1315.8 ?2,Loop 3贡献最大。竞争ELISA证明G-3-1与Ephrin B2和m102.4(靶向RBD的抗体)完全竞争结合RBP,而与靶向非RBD表位的HENV-32、nAH1.3和hAH1.3无竞争。丙氨酸扫描突变实验表明,NiVM-RBP中F458和G506残基对其结合敏感,HeV-RBP中敏感残基更多,该差异可能与其NiV偏向的中和活性有关。综合结果表明G-3-1的表位位于RBP头部的受体结合域(RBD),其机制是阻断RBP与Ephrin B2受体的结合。 **四、RBP和F靶向C-Nab的串联融合增强中和广度和效力。** 研究人员利用刚性(AP)12连接子将靶向RBP的G-3-1与靶向F蛋白的C-Nab 2A1-3-8串联,构建双特异性纳米抗体2A1-3-8-(AP)12-G-3-1。在连接子优化过程中,刚性连接子(EAAAK)n和(AP)n优于柔性连接子(G4S)n,且2A1-3-8位于N端、G-3-1位于C端的长刚性连接子(AP)12效果最佳。与单克隆抗体2A1-3-8和G-3-1相比,2A1-3-8-(AP)12-G-3-1对NiVM、NiVB和HeV的中和活性表现出更高效力和更均衡的特征,其对NiVM和NiVB的活性较2A1-3-8分别提高1.3倍和6.0倍,较G-3-1分别提高11.5倍、18.7倍和1015.8倍。 **五、2A1-3-8-(AP)12-G-3-1有效预防小鼠NiV假病毒感染。** 研究人员建立了一种基于生物发光成像的BALB/c小鼠NiV假病毒感染模型,确定假病毒主要靶向脾脏,肺部和肝脏有较弱信号。预防实验中,在假病毒攻击前30分钟腹腔注射25 mg/kg抗体,结果显示所有抗体处理组(2A1-3-8、G-3-1、2A1-3-8-(AP)12-G-3-1和m102.4)均显著降低了脾脏、肺和肝脏中的病毒载量。2A1-3-8-(AP)12-G-3-1展现出色的预防活性,但在本实验剂量下未表现出显著优于单个C-Nab的保护效力。 **讨论与结论:** 讨论部分指出,纳米抗体具有组织穿透力强(如穿越血脑屏障)、生产成本低、可识别隐蔽表位等优势,但体内清除快是其主要限制。G-3-1-HLE仅提供50%保护,可能与其本身中和活性不够强或半衰期仍相对有限有关。RBD是NiV RBP上的免疫优势表位,针对RBD的抗体最为丰富且高效。鉴于单靶点抗体的逃逸风险,同时靶向RBP和F蛋白的双特异性抗体策略具有重要意义。连接子的选择对双特异性抗体功能至关重要,本研究通过系统优化确定了最佳连接子。双特异性抗体可能通过同时结合同一病毒颗粒上的两种包膜蛋白,或交联不同病毒颗粒发挥中和作用,但具体机制仍需进一步验证。研究局限性包括:未在真实病毒模型中进行剂量滴定和预防/治疗效果的全面评估、未对双特异性抗体抗逃逸突变能力进行直接验证。结论部分指出,该双特异性纳米抗体2A1-3-8-(AP)12-G-3-1不仅具有强效且平衡的NiV和HeV中和活性,还在小鼠模型中提供了有效的假病毒预防保护,为应对未来NiV暴发提供了有前景的候选分子,并为下一代双抗原靶向双特异性抗体的设计提供了宝贵策略。 news.content: 今日动态 返回首页 会员注册 登录 生物通快讯免费订阅 首页 今日动态 人才市场 新技术专栏 中国科学人 云展台 BioHot 定制我的BioHot 进入我的BioHot 进入我的集采 肿瘤癌症研究 免疫/基因/细胞疗法 神经生物学 健康与疾病 衰老机制与长寿 单细胞技术 基因编辑-CRISPR RNA研究 肠道菌与人体微生态 细胞代谢 AI生物信息学 COVID 云讲堂直播 会展中心 特价专栏 技术快讯 免费试用 生物通官微 陪你抓住生命科技 跳动的脉搏 生物通首页 > 今日动态 > 正文 康尼伐普坦竞争性抑制尼帕病毒基质蛋白:结合口袋动态与蛋白-膜相互作用的调控机制 《Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics》:Competitive Inhibition of the Nipah Virus Matrix Protein by Conivaptan: From Binding Pocket Dynamics to Protein-Membrane InteractionsOpen Access 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年10月11日 来源:Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics 2.9 编辑推荐: 自尼帕病毒首次出现以来,反复爆发使得寻找有效抗病毒疗法的努力不断升级。基质蛋白是一种关键的结构蛋白,维持病毒粒子架构,并在将病毒锚定到宿主质膜过程中发挥重要作用。磷脂酰肌醇4,5-二磷酸(PIP2)与基质蛋白的结合促进构象变化,从而促进膜结合并启动病毒组装。因此,有效的分子抑 义翘神州可提供高活性、高纯度细胞因子,支持类器官研究,欢迎下载详细技术资料! 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 Paper Open Access 自尼帕病毒首次出现以来,反复爆发使得寻找有效抗病毒疗法的努力不断升级。基质蛋白是一种关键的结构蛋白,维持病毒粒子架构,并在将病毒锚定到宿主质膜过程中发挥重要作用。磷脂酰肌醇4,5-二磷酸(PIP2)与基质蛋白的结合促进构象变化,从而促进膜结合并启动病毒组装。因此,有效的分子抑制剂不仅应与PIP2竞争尼帕病毒基质蛋白(NiVM)的结合位点,还应破坏其与宿主膜的相互作用。通过对FDA批准药物进行虚拟筛选并结合系综对接方法,我们鉴定出康尼伐普坦是尼帕病毒基质蛋白的潜在抑制剂。康尼伐普坦的多价相互作用在PIP2结合口袋中建立了稳定结合,同时重新调控蛋白-膜相互作用。在PIP2存在下,NiVM通过多个带电荷残基锚定于膜,导致明显的局部双分子层变形,这是膜重塑的早期特征。相比之下,康尼伐普坦结合减弱了膜锚定,保持了更加有序和致密的双分子层结构,从而抑制膜变形。综上所述,这些发现表明康尼伐普坦是一种有前景的尼帕病毒基质蛋白再利用抑制剂,并为靶向病毒组装过程中病毒-膜相互作用提供了机制框架。该内容仅可通过PDF获取。PDF:康尼伐普坦对尼帕病毒基质蛋白的竞争性抑制:从结合口袋动态到蛋白-膜相互作用?
